cards.question: What is the difference between CI, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment?
cards.answer: CI: automatically builds and tests every commit. Continuous Delivery: ensures every passing build is ready to deploy but requires manual approval. Continuous Deployment: every passing build is deployed to production automatically without human intervention.
keyPoints: CI: automatic build + test on every commit
Continuous Delivery: deployable at any time, manual release
Continuous Deployment: auto-deploys every passing build
All three require automated tests as quality gate

cards.question: How do GitHub Actions workflows work?
cards.answer: A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/. Triggered by events (push, pull_request, schedule). Contains jobs which run in parallel by default. Each job has steps that run sequentially. Jobs can declare dependencies with 'needs' to run sequentially.
keyPoints: Triggered by events: push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch
Jobs run in parallel by default; 'needs' creates dependency order
Steps run sequentially within a job
Secrets stored in GitHub Settings, accessed as ${{ secrets.NAME }}

cards.question: What deployment strategies exist and when to use them?
cards.answer: Blue-Green: two identical environments, instant switch, easy rollback. Canary: gradually route small percentage to new version, catch issues early. Rolling: replace instances one by one with zero downtime. Feature flags: decouple deployment from release.
keyPoints: Blue-Green: instant switch, requires 2x resources, easy rollback
Canary: gradual traffic shift, detects issues with limited blast radius
Rolling: zero downtime, briefly runs two versions simultaneously
Feature flags: deploy code to all, control visibility per user/group

cards.question: How is Docker used in CI/CD pipelines?
cards.answer: Docker packages the application and all dependencies into an image, ensuring the same artifact runs identically in CI, staging, and production. Multi-stage builds produce small production images. Images pushed to registry and pulled by deployment targets.
keyPoints: Immutable artifact: same image tested and deployed
Multi-stage builds: build in full image, copy to minimal runtime image
Container registry stores versioned images (ECR, GCR, Docker Hub)
.dockerignore reduces image size and build context

cards.question: What are the three pillars of observability?
cards.answer: Metrics: numerical measurements over time (latency, error rate, CPU). Logs: timestamped records of discrete events for debugging. Traces: track a request across multiple services to identify bottlenecks. Together they answer: what's wrong, why it happened, where across services.
keyPoints: Metrics: quantitative over time — Prometheus, Datadog
Logs: timestamped event records — structured JSON preferred
Traces: distributed request tracking — Jaeger, OpenTelemetry
Alert on symptoms (error rate), not causes (CPU spike)

cards.question: How do you optimize CI/CD pipeline speed?
cards.answer: Cache dependencies between runs to avoid reinstalling. Run jobs in parallel where possible. Use matrix builds for cross-environment testing. Only run relevant jobs based on changed files (path filtering). Use incremental builds and test only affected code.
keyPoints: Cache node_modules by package-lock.json hash
Parallel jobs: lint, typecheck, and test simultaneously
Path filtering: only run deploy job when src/ changes
Fail fast: run fastest checks (lint, typecheck) before slow tests

cards.question: How do you handle secrets and security scanning in CI/CD?
cards.answer: Store secrets in the platform's secret store (GitHub Secrets, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) — never commit them to code. Use OIDC-based authentication to cloud providers instead of long-lived keys. Run dependency scanning (npm audit, Snyk) and SAST tools in the pipeline as mandatory gates.
keyPoints: Never commit secrets — use platform secret stores
OIDC short-lived tokens vs long-lived service account keys
Dependency scanning: npm audit, Snyk, Dependabot in CI
SAST/DAST tools scan code and running app for vulnerabilities

cards.question: How do you reuse logic across multiple GitHub Actions workflows?
cards.answer: Composite actions bundle multiple steps into a reusable action defined in action.yml. Reusable workflows allow calling an entire workflow from another workflow using the workflow_call trigger. Both reduce duplication and keep pipelines DRY across repositories.
keyPoints: Composite action: reusable steps, lives in .github/actions/ or separate repo
Reusable workflow: triggered via workflow_call, can pass inputs and secrets
Public actions from Marketplace: uses: actions/checkout@v4
Pin actions to SHA for security: uses: actions/checkout@abc123

cards.question: What is a rollback strategy and when should you use it?
cards.answer: A rollback restores a previous stable version when a deployment causes errors. Strategies: redeploy previous image tag (container), revert the commit and redeploy, use blue-green's instant traffic switch. Trigger rollbacks automatically based on error rate thresholds. Database migrations must be backward-compatible to allow rollback.
keyPoints: Immutable images: previous tag can be redeployed instantly
Blue-Green: rollback = switch load balancer back to blue
Automated rollback: error rate > threshold triggers revert
DB migrations must be backward-compatible to allow safe rollback

cards.question: What is environment parity and why does it matter?
cards.answer: Environment parity means dev, staging, and production use the same OS, runtime version, dependencies, and configuration structure. Differences between environments cause 'works on my machine' bugs. Docker and infrastructure-as-code (Terraform) enforce parity. The 12-factor app principle states: config in environment variables, not code.
keyPoints: Same Docker image runs in CI, staging, and production
Config via environment variables — never hardcoded
.env.example committed; .env gitignored
Infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, CDK) provisions identical environments
